claim_grade: B (empirical, peer-reviewed). Tier 1: recognised-scholar peer-reviewed venue (Springer Nature, Faculty of Economics, Thammasat University authors). Caveats: model-based/accounting (SPA is 'not intended to estimate causal effects'); land-rent split is the authors' own estimate; counterfactuals are stylised reallocations, not a tax.
content_summary: Data (s.4): new SAM built on NESDC's 2015 Input-Output table (180 sectors aggregated to 18), 51 accounts, plus NESDC National Income accounts and the NSO Household Socio-Economic Survey (HSES); households in five income quintiles (household 5 = richest). First Thai SAM to split land rent from capital (prior SAMs use capital and labour only). Land rent measurement (s.4, Eqs 15-16, App. B): value added = wages + gross operating surplus; land rent is estimated either as rent per unit area x land area used by activity, or as a fixed percentage of land value; capital return = operating surplus + depreciation - land rent. Land payments: to government from 'general government property income receivable' in National Income; to firms = firm land value x estimated rent rate; to households = residual, allocated across quintiles by HSES rent-income distribution. Concentration figures: the paper does NOT report a Gini for land-rent income vs labour/capital income. It cites Laovakul (2016) for a land-ownership Gini 'as high as 0.88' and 'the top ten landholders own 61% of all titled land' (s.1), national income Gini 0.430 (2021) vs 0.487 (1988) (s.1, NESDC), richest 1% ~58% of wealth (Ridzuan et al. 2021). Its own concentration evidence is path-level: e.g. agriculture->land total effects 0.001/0.0027/0.0256 for households 3/4/5 and zero for households 1-2 (s.5.1.1); real estate->land 0.0018/0.0048/0.0456 (s.5.1.2); manufacturing land rent goes to household 5 only (s.5.1.3); accommodation/food land rent to households 4-5 only (s.5.1.4); mining concentrated in top three, mainly household 5 (s.5.1.5). Capital for comparison: real estate->capital 0.2329 (hh5) vs 0.0048 (hh1); agriculture->capital 0.1658 vs 0.0034; labour more even. Headline: land rent is the most unequally distributed factor income. Structural paths (s.5.1): five highest-land-rent sectors = agriculture, real estate, manufacturing, accommodation and food services, mining. Agriculture and manufacturing raise land demand only indirectly (agriculture via manufacturing; manufacturing via agriculture, mining, trade, finance); real estate and mining show no indirect land effects through other sectors; accommodation/food affects land only via agriculture. Land has the fewest and weakest indirect pathways of the three factors; capital the most. Counterfactuals (s.5.2): reallocate 10% (scenario 1) or 25% (scenario 2) of the richest household group's land rent to households 1-4 in shares 35/35/25/5%. Baseline: richest household gets ~37-40x the poorest's sectoral multiplier. Scenario 1: ~35x. Scenario 2: poorest household's multipliers rise from 0.013/0.0108/0.007/0.0098/0.0051 to 0.0151/0.014/0.0075/0.0107/0.0056 (agriculture, real estate, manufacturing, accommodation & food, mining); real estate +30% (0.0108->0.0140), agriculture +16%, others <=10%; richest household's multipliers fall by no more than ~1%; richest/poorest multiplier ratio falls 24% in real estate, 15% in agriculture, <10% elsewhere. Baseline: the two poorest households' direction of effect is negative in all five sectors (regressive); under scenario 2, agriculture and real estate demand become progressive for all households. Abstract: 'redistributing land rent income can significantly reduce income inequality' - the paper's measured effects are modest (ratio ~37-40x to ~35x in scenario 1), so 'significantly' is the authors' wording, not a large effect. Policy discussion mentions redistributive land policies generally; not framed as an LVT paper.

suggested_text: A 2025 structural path analysis of Thailand's economy, built on a Social Accounting Matrix that separates land rent from capital returns, found land rent to be the most unequally distributed factor income, flowing almost entirely to the richest household groups. In the authors' simulation, shifting 25% of the richest group's land rent to poorer households raised the poorest group's real-estate sector multiplier by about 30% while lowering the richest group's by no more than about 1%.
